item.title: Tutorial: Getting started with the Molecular Simulation Workspace
item.description: When I started my PhD research I came with a heavy background in Physics, some computation experience (mostly in C) but my training had been in overwhelmingly in theoretical and statistical physics. So when I started working on Viruses and specifically running molecular dynamics simulations on proteins saying I was a bit lost is an understatement. It took me a few weeks just to even get up setup with VMD and preview the proteins I would be working with for the next 4 years (shoutout to 6UI7, 1QGT and 2G33). It took me a few more weeks to understand MD simulations, get setup with NAMD, understand errors like atoms moving too fast, simulation unstable and be able to visualize any kind of small fluctuation in protein structure. With the help of LLMs this learning curve has probably become way easier for new grad students. But what I wanted to use this simulation agent and MolScript is to be able to visualize these without even installing any softwares for the first time. I think the first step to learning is seeing and trust me there is no joy like being able to visualize your protein fluctuating on a computer screen for the first time. So this is just a guided tutorial for getting setup and started quickly for a quick preview of your protein of choice.This tutorial generally follows the steps mentioned in this NAMD tutorial.

item.title: Finding my written voice
item.description:
Writing for a non-native speaker can be difficult. While I’m very good at conversations and comprehension, writing in English feels unnatural to me. Writing and editing my thesis was one of the most challenging parts of my PhD.

For the longest time, even when I could express my thoughts, grammar and spotting what sounded weird were difficult for me to recognize. Scientific writing sometimes came easily because I was supposed to follow certain structures, terminologies, and wording. But things did get lost in translation. Even with Grammarly double-checking everything, I felt like it was yet another restriction on writing regularly.

item.title: Why I Love Markov State Models (And So Should You)
item.description:
Markov State Models (MSMs) are one of those mathematical tools that, once you understand them, you start seeing applications everywhere. As someone who has used them extensively in my research, I wanted to share why I find them so powerful and versatile. Over the course of this post, we’ll explore their history, fundamentals, and applications that extend far beyond their traditional use in computational biochemistry.

A Brief History

The foundation for what we now call Markov processes was laid by Russian mathematician Andrey Markov in 1906. His work on chains of dependent random variables would eventually become one of the most important concepts in probability theory and has applications spanning from weather prediction to protein folding.

item.title: My lessons from gaming
item.description:
For anyone who knows me, my absolute lack of hand-eye coordination is pretty obvious. A scooter ride gone bad in high school, left me with a half functioning elbow and two neourologically numb fingers on my left hand.

One of the biggest reason that I’m a strictly computational scientist is my extremely shaky hands and general propensity to drop things. I think the most challenging course for me was my second year Optics lab course at IITK. I cannot count the number of times I almost broke during down lab because I couldn’t align the lenses properly. I think the weeks working on Michaelson Interferometer where one of the most difficult weeks of my life. To Prof. Saikat Ghosh my instructor, and Smit Choudhay my labmate if you ever come across my blog I owe you me passing that course. Hence, began a hate relationship with experiments. Luckily for me, I loved math which meant I did not have to give up my dreams of becoming a physicist.

item.title: My first blogpost: This time for sure
item.description:
I have a confession to make. This website has been in the development stage for more than a year. I have had a layout ready this whole time. I figured out how to make Hugo work to my liking for months. But the “rate determining step” has been my apprehension to write that first post.

I have never written a blog post, countless dear diary entries sure but I haven’t ever put my partially cooked thoughts out on the internet before. And when I say that I mean I am one of those quite internet lurkers. Upon some self reflection I have realized a couple of reasons for this. The first one is I never thought I was interesting enough. I don’t like saying something when I believe I’m not bringing anything new to the conversation. I believed in a world where almost everyone shares their opinions on everything, my perspective was not unique. Maybe that’s still true but as a true 21st century human I have to try shouting my thoughts at the internet void anyway. The other reason was I’m a perfectionist, it’s a problem but I hate making mistakes. And English is my third language, so that means making lots of grammatical mistakes. As a sidenote if you spot any let me know! I’m trying not to use ChatGPT and using this as a writing exercise. And this lack of fluency made me even more nervous about blogging.
